WhatFun · design exploration · three studios, one brief

Riffs on the pinwheel

The current icon (left) stays the reference: six hand-placed cards, media glyphs, and the negative-space sparkle you like. Every exploration below keeps that DNA and answers one piece of your feedback — single-hue progressive shades, etched glyphs, new center shapes, dark mode throughout, and a layered Icon Composer rebuild.

Final · approved

The WhatFun icon

Your composed configuration, baked exactly as the configurator rendered it: a warm-to-cool six-hue wheel (vermilion, tangerine, ochre, teal, cornflower, lavender), warm-white radial ground at 37% depth, no glow, mark at 84% with a 4° tilt, star opened +22, corners rounded to 90, glyphs at 103% size with 225% hand-tilt and 143% emboss. The dark build is a derived proposal (each hue lifted 8% on a warm near-black ground) — tweakable in the configurator if it isn’t right. This design now ships as the app’s AppIcon.png, and the AppIcon.icon Composer bundle has been rebuilt to match.

Round 7 · the winner, tuned

Rim glow, navy dark, and a live configurator

Your G5 verdict applied: the radial blob is gone. The glow is now geometry-locked to the star — a soft luminous fringe hugging only the star’s edges, with the star’s interior a different colour from the ground (“different colour in the middle”). Pixel-probed in dark mode: the background stays flat and the petals stay exactly their hex right up to the cutout — no wash. Dark ground is now ink-navy #0D1430 (the bluer #122048 was tried and rejected: it crowds the indigo petal and softens the mark’s pop at small sizes). For rotating the petal colours and tuning everything live, use the interactive configurator published alongside this page — it renders from the same geometry and can download the exact SVG you compose.

H1Rim glow · amber

The winner spec: bright hues, porcelain light / ink-navy dark, amber rim glow with a warm-cream star interior (lifted navy interior in dark). At 64 px the dark mode reads as a spark, the light as a warm-white star.

H3Rim glow · coral

The alternative glow colourway: hot coral in light, rose in dark, with matching star interiors. Punchier, slightly less classic than amber.

The subtle inside→outside porcelain gradient (#F8F8F4 → #E9EAE5) — far quieter than G4’s aged-paper look. The gradient depth is adjustable in the configurator.

Round 6 · vivid spectrum, refined

Brighter hues, cleaner grounds, a glowing star

All six variants have the glyphs moved 10% inward as requested. The variants isolate each of your questions: a control, a brighter hue tuning, a non-beige ground, your gradient-background idea, your star-glow idea, and a combo of the winners. Verdict on the beige: partly guilty — A/B-ing cream against porcelain shows the cream’s yellow cast visibly dirties the cool half of the wheel (indigo, violet, teal all clean up on porcelain), while the warm petals never suffered — which is why ember always looked fine on it.

G1Base (control)

F1’s exact hues with only the glyph shift, on cream. The inward glyphs are a clear win — the petal corners breathe again — but the ink-deep hues now read reserved next to the bright set.

G2Bright

#4A63E4#9550D6#E0339B#F04A32#E2621F#12A38C

Backlit candy: saturation and lightness up, still nowhere pale (greyscale-checked). Confirms “brighter” was right; only the cream ground holds it back.

G3Cool ground

The bright hues on porcelain #F1F2EF (light) and neutral near-black #131417 (dark). If you want zero gradient trickery, this is the honest winner — crispest of all at 64 px.

G4Gradient ground

Your idea: radial ground, luminous ivory centre falling to a cooler stone edge, so the star is the brightest thing on the canvas. The dark mode (violet centre-glow to near-black) is the best single dark file this round; the light mode reads slightly like aged paper at small sizes.

G5Star glow

Your other idea: a soft halo behind the petals bleeding through the star cutout — hot ember core in dark mode. Works, but on cream the glow is timid; the idea lives on better in G6.

G6Combo

Bright hues at their cleanest on porcelain, plus a whisper of the warm star-core in both modes. The warm/cool tension makes the sparkle the focal point — which is the icon’s whole idea. The designer’s pick.

Round 5 · vivid multi-hue

Saturation up, no pale cards, no yellow

Your steer applied: the monochromatic ramps are retired, and these five schemes take the spectrum idea further — chroma pushed clearly higher, the whole value band biased deeper so nothing reads pale against the cream, and yellow banned outright. Same icon-grid construction as Round 4. Every scheme passed a greyscale check so no petal jumps forward, and the letterpress etch was re-tuned per scheme to survive the saturation.

F1Vivid spectrum

#4257C2#8244B5#C22B85#D8402E#BC4F1C#0E7D6C

The direct answer to “more like spectrum, more saturated”: six rich hues in spectral order, indigo to forest teal, no yellow or olive. Disciplined and iconic.

F2Sunset

#D4562F#D8404C#C92F67#A82E82#7C3193#462D8C

Your analogous fix, verbatim: the golden step deleted, burnt coral sweeping through raspberry and magenta to deep indigo. Keeps the progressive rotation the pinwheel was built for. The designer’s top pick.

F3Retro pop

#40578F#A84D1C#16766F#B33A2B#2E6B33#AF2D6E

70s board-game box: every seam is a complementary bounce (navy/orange, orange/teal, teal/brick…), so each card pops without any hue dominating. The most characterful.

F4Jewel

#1D4E9E#B01E42#0C7048#8C4E1B#71399C#8A2433

Sapphire, ruby, emerald, amber, amethyst, garnet — the deepest band, with the etch depth boosted to stay legible. Luxurious and the best dark-mode set, but trades away some “fun.”

F5Neon dusk

#2C55C0#D6248E#0A8278#C63F26#6931B8#B01E55

Arcade-cabinet energy with strict cool/hot alternation. Superb in dark mode; slightly restless at home-screen size next to the calmer orders.

Round 4 · A1v2 at icon-grid size

Right-sized, five ways

The v2 pinwheel rescaled to Apple’s HIG icon-grid circle: the mark now occupies a ≈762 px footprint on the 1024 canvas — flat petal edges at ≈720 px, corner peaks kissing the 768 px reference ring the way the Settings gear’s teeth do — instead of the previous ≈920 px sprawl. Construction is otherwise identical to A1v2 (squircle sixth glyph, letterpress etch, sparkle). Five palettes, all value-disciplined so the lightest card holds against the background.

E1Ember

#EFA758#E98C48#E0713C#D05532#B33E28#8C2B1F

The approved v2 ramp, rescaled — the control. Most legible stepping of the five at 64 px, and the warmest “fun.”

E2Ocean

#8FCEC2#63B8AD#3F9D97#26807F#155F66#0C424C

The round-1 teal rebalanced v2-style. Impeccably legible and calm, though it reads a touch corporate next to the warm options.

E3Analogous

#EFA93F#F0854A#E96350#D74863#AC3672#7C2A6B

Golden → coral → raspberry → plum. The strongest new candidate: keeps ember’s warmth but the raspberry deep-end gives the ramp a livelier arc and the top golden card real presence.

E4Spectrum

#7395CA#AF7FB5#E8785A#CB8E3C#8CA463#5AAEA6

Six hues in spectral order, greyscale-matched (±8 lightness band) so none jumps forward; denim takes the top squircle card. Genuinely harmonious — but note it quietly reintroduces the multi-colour idea you originally rejected. The deliberate outlier.

E5Twilight

#96A6DC#7A87CE#5F65B8#48489E#353080#232052

The designer’s pick: periwinkle → deep indigo on warm paper. Atmospheric, “reading at midnight” — distinctive against a home screen full of blue apps because of the warm ground.

Round 3 · Ember, fixed

The top card earns its place

Your two notes on A1 applied: the whole six-step ramp is rebalanced (not just the first step darkened) so the lightest card separates cleanly from the cream, and the formerly blank top petal now carries a sixth glyph — a generic app squircle with a centre dot, etched in the same letterpress style, reading as “everything else.” Two rebalances to choose from. The Icon Composer push is further down in Exploration C, fully refreshed with the same fixes.

A1 v2Ember v2

#EFA758#E98C48#E0713C#D05532#B33E28#8C2B1F

The recommended fix: the ladder shifts down half a step with even perceptual spacing preserved. The top card now separates cleanly from both grounds at 120 px.

A1 v3Ember v3

#E8973F#E28839#D66C34#C24F2D#A03824#75251B

The moodier alternative: a tight amber pair at the top and a longer run into near-burgundy — more presence up top, more molten overall.

Round 2 · the star

The rating star, lapped

Your notes applied to B3: the cards now physically overlap — each laps the previous, the deepest closing the loop over the lightest for one deliberate seam — and the whole mark is scaled to Apple’s icon-grid proportion (740 px circle on the 1024 canvas) instead of running edge-to-edge. Glyphs carry the full letterpress emboss from the A set. The star is subtracted from every card before rounding, so no lap edge can nibble a point. Five palette schemes, from the familiar single ramp to full trips around the colour wheel.

D1Ember mono

#FFB491#FF9268#F76F4A#DC4F30#AE3722

The single-hue control. Strongest star legibility of the five — the value ramp does all the work — but the least distinctive on a busy home screen.

D2Analogous

#F2B24E#F28E52#EF6B55#DE4E68#B93D77

A warm sweep from golden through coral to raspberry: hue moves, lightness stays even. The most “WhatFun” of the set — richer than mono while keeping one-family cohesion.

D3Spectrum

#E8785A#D0923F#8CA463#55A8A0#AC7DB2

Five media, five hues around the wheel — the tasteful heir to the original multicolour icon. Values are matched (greyscale-checked) so no card jumps forward and the star owns the mark. The designer’s top pick.

D4Duotone

#FF8A5C#2E8C89#F2653C#16646B#C43D20

Complementary coral/teal split 3 / 2 — the boldest poster read, though the two teal cards pair up visually and slightly fight the five-fold rhythm at small sizes.

D5Jewel

#D8933B#B23A48#7C4FA3#3C6DB0#2F8F6B

The designer’s wildcard: a night spectrum of jewel tones. Cinematic and premium in dark mode; the cooler cast drifts furthest from the app’s warm personality.

Round 1 · Exploration A

Progressive shades, etched glyphs

One hue family per icon, six petals stepping light → deep clockwise from the blank top card. The glyphs are now debossed: tone-on-tone fills with a 1–2 px highlight/shadow fringe, so they read as pressed into the card — visible up close, invisible noise-free at home-screen size. The 64 px thumbnails under each tile are the honest small-size check.

A1Ember

#F6BE6E#F2A054#EA8044#DE5F38#C4432C#9C2F23

The evolution of the existing brand: the mixed palette resolved into one apricot-to-brick sunset ramp. Keeps WhatFun’s warmth and stays the most recognisable as the same app.

A2Ocean

#ABDCD2#7AC6BB#4FABA4#2E8C89#1A6A6E#104A54

Teal carries the widest legible lightness range of any hue family, so the six steps stay distinct at every size. The designer’s pick for the cleanest progressive stepping — calm and very iOS-native.

A3Plum

#E5BAD0#D496BE#BF74A9#A35590#823C76#5D2A5C

Evening-media mood — movie night, late-night reading. The pink-to-aubergine ramp has the strongest single-hue drama of the four.

A4Moss

#C2CF9E#A8BC83#8DA669#728E54#587440#3F582F

Bookish, botanical calm, nodding to the sage card in the current icon. The quietest option; its mid-steps compress slightly at thumbnail size.

Exploration B

What else can the center say?

Same pinwheel language, same ember ramp — but the petal tips are re-carved so the negative space forms a different mark. Nothing is drawn in the middle; the background genuinely shows through, exactly like the sparkle today.

B1Play button

Six petals whose seams land on the triangle’s vertices and side midpoints, keeping the corners sharp. Play is the universal “press to enjoy” of media — the strongest single symbol for an entertainment tracker. Unmistakable at 64 px.

B2Aperture

Six overlapping shutter blades form a hexagonal iris — the glyph-free, purely geometric variation. The shade-stepped overlaps create the swirl on their own; opening the iris is a nice metaphor for opening the app to see what’s next.

B3Rating star

Five petals at 72°, each tip carving one concave notch; the star’s points bleed into the seams exactly like the sparkle you already love. The app rates in half-stars, so the negative space now says “track and rate what you love.” The most legible of the set at small sizes.

B4Heart

Mirror-symmetric: the top petal’s tip splits into two prongs to own the cleft — the FedEx-arrow moment of the set — and the deepest shade wraps the point. Favourites made literal. Reads better in dark mode; if it advances, the ramp should start darker in light mode.

Round 3 · Exploration C, further

The Icon Composer rebuild

Refreshed per your notes and pushed further: the ramp starts deeper, the top wedge carries the new squircle glyph, and the glass simulation gained a specular rim, inner bevel, and dark-mode edge glow. Below the four dynamic modes: the separated layers, two home-screen context mockups at realistic tile size, and a best-effort AppIcon.icon bundle you can try opening in Icon Composer.

  • AppIcon.icona ready-made bundle (icon.json + layer assets) sits beside the layer sources. The JSON schema was cross-checked against an open-source project that reads real Icon Composer bundles, but it couldn’t be opened in Icon Composer from here — treat it as a head start; if anything looks off on open, the drag-in-three-layers path in the notes is the reliable route.
  • The sparkleis a hole in the petal layer, not a drawn shape. Default: carved into glass. Dark: inverts to a dark star. Clear: a literal window to the wallpaper. Tilting the phone parallaxes it deeper than the petals — for free.
  • Petal layerspecular on, soft neutral shadow, all six petals in one group so glass treats them as a single slab.
  • Glyph layerspecular off, shadow minimal — the layer’s parallax lift sells the deboss on its own.
  • Why one hue winsTinted mode maps luminance to the user’s tint, so a single-hue lightness ramp degrades perfectly to mono. The progressive-shades direction and the Composer direction reinforce each other.

Where things stand

  1. The final design is approved and shipped: it is now the app’s AppIcon.png, with the Icon Composer bundle rebuilt to match. Remaining manual step: open i-final/AppIcon.icon in Icon Composer on a Mac, confirm the layers and modes, and wire it into the Xcode target per c-composer/ICON-COMPOSER-NOTES.md.
  2. The dark build is a derived proposal — if it needs tuning, adjust in the configurator’s dark mode and send the readout.

All vector sources, generator scripts, and the Icon Composer wiring notes are committed under docs/icon-explorations/ on branch claude/icon-design-variations-ve59v4. Every icon above is shown in its light and dark build; flip this page’s theme to proof the gallery chrome both ways.
